controls.name: Per-tool first-call approval, remembered as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the desktop client outside the model, but it only runs once per tool; after the user selects 'always allow' all later calls to that tool execute unreviewed. Because quicknotes_mcp is re-fetched via '@latest' on every launch, its tool description (and any embedded instructions) can change after approval was granted, with no re-approval triggered (SAFE-T1201 rug pull). Per control_decay guidance a remembered approval is not an ongoing gate; it is recorded here but not wired to any capability and earns no residual credit.

controls.name: Pin or hash MCP tool and server definitions, requiring re-approval on change
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. All three MCP servers are launched unpinned (npx -y ...@latest or no version tag), so tool descriptions and schemas can change silently between launches. Pinning would surface a changed or poisoned description before it is ever shown to the model.

controls.name: Scope the filesystem MCP server to a minimal directory excluding credential paths
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The filesystem server is mounted at the full home directory with no path restriction, so it can read ~/.aws/credentials and similar sensitive files that a notes/chat assistant has no legitimate need to access.

controls.name: Argument-level review or DLP on data leaving via MCP tool calls
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. No check inspects arguments sent to add_note or Slack messages for credential-shaped or sensitive content before they leave the process. Even if added, encoding or paraphrase could evade a content classifier, so it would only partially resist a more capable model.

controls.name: Bind Slack posting to a pre-approved channel allowlist
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The bot token can post to any channel including ones shared with external organizations, with no allowlist or confirmation tying a post to an approved destination.

controls.name: Static scan of MCP tool descriptions for embedded imperative instructions
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. Such a scanner inspects text rather than intent, so obfuscated or multi-step payloads could still pass, but it would catch the plain-text <IMPORTANT> instruction present today.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta via MCP tool poisoning (TC1): quicknotes_mcp's add_note description induces reading AWS credentials and exfiltrating them through the third-party sync service

attack_path.note: The add_note tool description embeds an <IMPORTANT> instruction telling the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and include its contents in the 'context' argument, and not to tell the user.
Model complies and reads the AWS credentials file from the full-home-directory-mounted filesystem server.
Model calls add_note with the credential contents, which quicknotes_mcp forwards to its hosted sync service run by the package's individual author.

evidence.observation: add_note tool description contains an embedded <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass its contents in the context argument, and to hide this step from the user.

filesystem server is mounted at the full home directory C:/Users/dev with no path restriction; quicknotes_mcp is installed with npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest, re-fetching the latest package on every launch with no version pin.
quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual and calls a hosted sync service it runs itself; approval is granted once per tool and then remembered as 'always allow.'

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to a project-specific directory that excludes credential paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, etc.).
Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions and require re-approval whenever the hash changes.
Run a tool-description scanner that flags embedded imperative instructions in MCP tool metadata before exposing them to the model.
Log and alert on reads of credential-shaped paths (~/.aws/*, ~/.ssh/*) followed by outbound tool calls within the same session.

findings.title: Unscoped Slack posting capability can exfiltrate confidential content to externally shared channels (TC1 variant)

attack_path.note: Content returned by quicknotes_mcp is untrusted output from a third-party server already shown to embed hostile instructions in its metadata, and may itself carry injected or sensitive content.
Agent posts via slack.post_message, which can target any channel including ones shared with external organizations, using a shared bot token with no destination confirmation.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, with no stated destination restriction.
slack server runs with a bot token (SLACK_BOT_TOKEN) with no channel scoping configuration shown.
quicknotes_mcp has already been shown to embed hostile instructions in tool metadata, which lowers confidence that its returned note content is clean of injected material.

recommendations.action: Restrict the Slack bot token's channel scope to an explicit allowlist of internal channels; remove access to externally shared channels.
Require destination confirmation bound to a pre-approved channel list before posting, especially to externally shared channels.
Log outbound Slack posts and alert when posted content overlaps with data recently read via quicknotes or the filesystem tool in the same session.

rating.rationale: Two toxic combinations reach S3 sinks from untrusted sources with no effective preventive control in place. First, a textbook MCP tool-poisoning and rug-pull pattern (SAFE-T1001/SAFE-T1201): the unpinned, third-party quicknotes_mcp server's add_note description instructs the model to read AWS credentials from an unscoped filesystem mount and forward them to the author's own hosted sync service. Second, the Slack posting capability is unscoped (any channel, including externally shared ones) and can carry confidential or injected content from quicknotes output. The only control present, first-call approval remembered as 'always allow,' is not a real per-call gate and is further undermined because tool definitions are unpinned and refetched on every launch, so it earns no residual credit under the rubric. Inherent, residual, and forecast all sit at critical; there are no dependent or partially dependent controls left to decay further, because none of substance exist today.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration artifacts (mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list response, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt was provided, so the agent's own instructions could not be reviewed for additional issues such as ambiguous goals or unbounded scope.
Exact OS-level permissions behind the filesystem and Slack MCP servers were not independently verified; capability scope is inferred from mcp.json and the runtime notes.

The path from in.notes_output to cap.slack_post in finding f2 is inferred from typical assistant usage patterns rather than an explicit instruction in the artifacts, hence medium rather than high confidence.

No forecast-horizon findings were added because both present findings already sit at the ceiling tier (critical) and no additional controls remain whose decay would raise the tier further; if structural controls are added later (per the recommendations), this assessment should be rerun to establish a meaningful forecast.
